prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I still place the optical lattice clock first. It is a single, sharply defined invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors at once, and Ye's group carried it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 with ultrastable lasers and clock comparisons. Seven of eight members rank it in their top five and all eight propose the same two names, which is rare for attribution. Impact is concrete and measurable (second redefinition, relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter couplings), and independent confirmation at several institutes is complete, so neither originality, attribution nor maturity is in doubt. The two-person size also leaves room in the allocation that a crowded field such as twisted graphene or optical-lattice simulation does not.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is precision-measurement engineering built on prior recognised pillars: the frequency comb (2005) and ion control and ion clocks (2012). A committee could judge that a lattice clock is an improvement on an already honoured line, and the formal redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the biggest payoff is still prospective. Credit for the best results also rests on ultrastable cavity lasers and on other lattice-clock groups (for example Ludlow, Hinkley, Campbell, Takamoto) outside the two names. Finally, B001 has far stronger opening support (four first places) and may be the better choice for the scientific breadth of the field it opened.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a clean case of a concrete prediction (flat band at the magic angle) that nature then confirmed, with a stable physical picture after eight years, and sees the lattice clock as a clear, highly mature invention with a clear payoff.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is the cleanest theory-then-experiment sequence on the list, and I rank it highly enough to name it as my first alternative. My difference is about what is stable. The existence of flat-band correlated phases is robust, but the nature of the superconductivity and of several correlated states is still contested, and that makes me cautious about writing a citation that rests on interpretation. A citation for the clock has no such dependence: the claim is a measured number reproduced in Tokyo, Boulder, Braunschweig, Paris and elsewhere. On the 2005 overlap you raise, I would say the comb was the tool, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a new method of trapping that is distinct from it.

responses.point: Kroll places the lattice clock first as the clearest invention that changed what can be measured, and discloses a documented link to John Hall's laboratory and a past collaboration between Hall and Ye.
responses.response: I share the scientific assessment, and I think Kroll's disclosure is handled correctly: the Hall link is to a laureate already honoured for the comb, whereas the proposed names are Katori and Ye, so it is a point for transparency and not grounds to discount the case. Where I would qualify Kroll is on the attribution of Ye. His group's contribution is more than a continuation of the comb work: the many-body spin-exchange clock physics and the stability record are distinct, and that is why I treat the prize as Katori's concept plus Ye's demonstration of its limit. I am also less comfortable with the idea that Cirac and Zoller are an equal alternative if both would need to be split across B007 and B015 in one year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first but would name only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, noting that Bistritzer's omission is the price of a clean two-person prize, and he ranks the lattice clock fourth with a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: I would resist the two-name version of B001. Bistritzer and MacDonald wrote the 2011 continuum-model paper together and the magic angle is named for the calculation, so omitting Bistritzer would break the logic of crediting the prediction at all. If the committee goes to B001 I think the three credited names are the defensible set, with the experimental side still imperfect because Cao and Fatemi sit outside it. That asymmetry, a clean attribution for the clock and an unresolved one for twisted graphene, is a main reason I keep B007 ahead even though Mehlig and I agree that both are mature and timely.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and Cirac-Zoller second, and argues that a theory-only prize for ion and atom proposals is defensible because Wineland already has a prize, while noting that the 2025 circuit prize may argue for waiting on B058.
responses.response: I agree with Johansson on B015 on the merits: the 1995 gate proposal and the lattice and Rydberg proposals are original and have been realised on many platforms, so I rank it second. It is for this reason a good alternative, but I would not make it the preferred configuration, because a theory-only prize in a field whose experimental pioneers are mostly unrecognised or already recognised under another heading is harder to justify than a prize that joins invention and demonstration. On B058, I think Johansson's own point about 2025 is the stronger one, and Wallraff's omission from the credited names is a real fairness problem that three names cannot repair.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks optical-lattice simulation third with Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger, but flags Greiner's omission as a real attribution cost and the unanswered question whether analogue simulators have solved a problem classical methods cannot.
responses.response: I take both points seriously and they are the reason I keep B008 at fifth. The Mott-insulator experiment and the gas microscope are Greiner's as much as Bloch's, and a three-person cap cannot keep Zoller, Bloch, Esslinger and Greiner together. I also agree that the claim of solving open problems is still aspirational. This is a case where I would not want to settle the configuration in a hurry.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see a lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether a prize that recognises the clock should also consider ion-clock pioneers.
Whether the formal redefinition of the second (not yet decided) should be treated as a condition for maturity or as an adjacent policy matter.
Whether the credit for the ultrastable cavity lasers and for other lattice-clock groups should lead the committee to change the two-person configuration.
Whether the superconducting mechanism and correlated-state debate in twisted bilayer graphene will have settled enough to change my ranking of B001 relative to B007.
statement.conflict_note: For B007 (Katori, Ye) I find no specific conflict in my profile. For other shortlisted candidates, my documented ties are to the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and L'Huillier, none of which is among the names credited on B007, B001, B015, B023 or B058. B008 credits Tilman Esslinger of ETH Zurich, and my professional proximity to ETH and to atomic theory around Zoller and Cirac may warrant disclosure if B008 or B015 were taken up. The proposed prize for B007 does not require recusal.
